p083.lead: Through capture and purchase, ritual and plural marriage, to pair marriage: the footsteps of marriage, man’s most exalted institution.

p083.foot.text: Presented by the Chief of Seraphim stationed on Urantia

p083.s0.h: Introduction — Men and Women Will Not Live Without Each Other
p083.s0.b0: Paper 83 tells how the mating mores examined in the previous paper became an institution. Marriage began as the loose association of the horde and, after many variations, culminated in pair marriage, the union of one man and one woman to establish a home of the highest social order. Marriage has often been in jeopardy and has drawn heavily on property and religion for support, but the force that has safeguarded it all along is something simpler.
p083.s0.b2: The author sees the sex urge as the unrecognized agency that civilized the savage. A relationship begun in pursuit of self-gratification inevitably brings self-denial, altruistic duty, and the responsibilities of the home, and this process makes people think and finally leads them to love. Beneath this paper lies the paradox that an impulse rooted in selfishness becomes a school of unselfishness.
p083.s1.h: I. Marriage as a Societal Institution
p083.s1.b0: Marriage is the mechanism society designed to regulate the many relationships that grow out of the fact of bisexuality. It regulates individual sex relations and, in its older and original function, also regulates descent, inheritance, succession, and social order. The family and the property mores stabilize marriage, and pride, chivalry, duty, and religious convictions help.
p083.s1.b2: The author draws a clear line: religion should mightily influence marriage but should not try to control and regulate it exclusively. Primitive marriage was chiefly industrial, with little romantic love; husband and wife grew fond of each other by living and working together. Marriage became mutual, romantic, and ethical only gradually.
p083.s2.h: II–III. Courtship and Betrothal; Purchase and Dowry
p083.s2.b1: The primitive approach to marriage was force, not attraction, and just as raiding preceded trading, marriage by capture preceded marriage by contract. Mock elopements and mock captures are relics of that age, and the paper traces the custom of carrying the bride over the threshold to it as well. For a long time women had no say, but as civilization advanced they took a larger part in every stage of courtship, and love, romance, and personal choice were contributions of the Andites to the world.
p083.s2.b2: The ancients did not trust love and promises, so they sought to secure the union with property. The purchase price of a wife was a deposit that the husband forfeited in case of divorce or desertion. As civilization advanced, fathers disliked the appearance of selling their daughters and began giving the couple presents of equal value, and this became the dowry.

p083.s3.h: IV. The Wedding Ceremony — Community Witness and Rites Against Ghosts
p083.s3.b0: The wedding ceremony arose because marriage was not a decision of two people alone but an affair of the community. In an age without records, many witnesses were needed to publicize property and the status of children. What began as a mere public notice of living together grew into a ceremony of eating together, and the red man was the first to develop elaborate wedding celebrations.
p083.s3.b1: Childlessness was greatly feared, and barrenness was attributed to the machinations of spirits. Efforts to ensure fertility therefore tied marriage to magic and religious ritual. People used charms, consulted astrologers about the stars, and chose lucky days such as Thursday or the full moon; for a time the weddings of the wealthy were even accompanied by human sacrifice. The priest’s blessing of the marriage bed is far older than any formal wedding rite.

p083.s3.b3: That so much of a beautiful ceremony arose from fear invites us to reconsider how we treat ritual. The form may remain while its meaning changes. When today’s wedding becomes not a device for fooling ghosts but an occasion for promising responsibility before the community, its original communal meaning comes back to life.
p083.s4.h: V. Plural Marriages — The Long Stairway from Horde to Pair
p083.s4.b0: The forms of marriage did not reach monogamy all at once. The first step away from the promiscuity of the horde was that a woman belonged to only one man at a time; then came group marriage, plural wives, and the concubine mores. Because the regulation of sex and marriage ensured the survival of more children, family life advanced slowly but surely.

p083.s4.b2: The polygamous system recognized four kinds of wives: ceremonial or legal wives, wives of affection, concubines, and slave wives. The wife with status was not necessarily the wife who was loved. Taboos during pregnancy and nursing, hard labor that aged women early, and high infant mortality all encouraged plural wives, and an older wife sometimes asked for a younger one herself.
p083.s4.b4: The story of the chief who dismissed his harem and was killed by the outraged relatives of his wives is a vivid example of this sentence. Even in the right direction, overturning customs in haste provokes fierce resistance. Reform needs time and wisdom as much as it needs ideals.
p083.s5.b0: The author does not romanticize monogamy. It is monopoly, a cultural and social product that is not natural to evolving man. The earliest monogamy arose from poverty. Yet it was wholly natural to the Nodites and Adamites, and it has been of great cultural value to all advanced races.
p083.s5.b2: Because this ideal requires self-denial, it often fails for lack of that acme of human virtues, rugged self-control. Monogamy fosters refined sentiment, moral character, and spiritual growth, and the paper adds that a woman cannot be an ideal mother while she must constantly compete for her husband’s affection. Above all, it is unquestionably best for the children.
p083.s5.b3: Notice the paper’s concern for those left outside this ideal. People who do not find a mate are easily left in the chill of a solitary existence, so the more fortunate majority should always treat them with kindness and consideration. Holding the ideal high and embracing those who do not reach it must go together.
p083.s6.h: VII. The Dissolution of Wedlock — Conditions That Lead to Divorce
p083.s6.b0: Among primitive peoples only about half of all marriages were satisfactory, and the most common reason for divorce was barrenness. Wife purchase and the dowry greatly reduced divorce by attaching property penalties to failure. In modern times, love, a more idealistic but extremely individualistic motive, suddenly replaced the older property motive, and marriage became temporarily unstable.
p083.s6.b1: Marriage has advanced steadily over the centuries, yet dissatisfaction has spread most widely precisely where the new freedom of personal choice operates most strongly. In every age the real test of marriage has been the continuous intimacy that family life makes unavoidable. Two people brought up to expect only self-gratification will find it hard to succeed in a lifelong partnership of compromise, devotion, and child rearing.

p083.s6.b3: The author warns that easy divorce returns society to cruder stages, yet acknowledges that as long as society fails to prepare young people for marriage, divorce must serve as a safety valve that prevents worse conditions. It is a balanced view that puts more weight on education than on blame.
p083.s7.h: VIII. The Idealization of Marriage — Humanly Divine
p083.s7.b1: The author considers it unfortunate that marriage has been called a sacrament or compared to the relation of the Adjuster and man, or of Michael and his brethren. The belief that marriages are consummated by divine action leads to the idea that they can never be dissolved, but the very fact that dissolution occurs shows that God was not the party who made the union. Spiritual progress can occur in marriage, but it occurs just as well along other paths.
p083.s7.b2: None of this lowers the ideal of marriage. On the headquarters of the local systems the Material Sons and Daughters actually portray the ideal of the union of man and woman, and the ideal mortal marriage is humanly sacred. The young person’s idealization of marriage is a picture of the future that should not be crushed, but it should be tempered by learning about reality. Nor should new forms of marriage go to the extreme of a mutual monopoly of personality and individuality.
p083.s8.b0: Paper 83 does not wrap marriage in a veil of mystery; it shows it plainly as a human institution. Doing so actually makes the responsibilities of marriage clearer. Heaven will not guard it for us; the self-control, devotion, and preparation of two people are what guard a marriage. Marriage began in crude coercion, but it can grow into a magnificent institution of self-culture.

p083.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 84, “Marriage and Family Life,” builds on the marriage institution described here to examine the partnership of man and woman, the growth of the family, and the ideals the home is to realize.
p084.lead: From the nucleus of mother and child to the home of pair marriage: the partnership of man and woman, the ideals of family life, and the self-gratification that threatens them.

p084.foot.text: Presented by the Chief of Seraphim stationed on Urantia

p084.s0.h: Introduction — The Channel of Culture and Knowledge
p084.s0.b0: Following two papers on the evolution of marriage, Paper 84 examines its fruit, the home. The author sums up the story of marriage in a single sentence: material necessity founded it, sex hunger embellished it, religion sanctioned and exalted it, the state demanded and regulated it, and in later times evolving love has begun to glorify it as the creator of the home.
p084.s0.b2: Individuals are very temporary as planetary factors, but the family is a continuing agency of social evolution. The home is the one institution that embraces all three essential functions of human existence: self-maintenance, self-perpetuation, and self-gratification. This paper follows that institution from its beginnings toward its ideals.
p084.s1.h: I. Primitive Pair Associations — The Nucleus of Mother and Child
p084.s1.b0: Marriage did not grow out of sex relations. Primitive man could satisfy his sex desires without responsibility, and he did not even know the connection between sex relations and childbirth. People believed that babies were made in the spirit world and that pregnancy came when a spirit entered a woman’s body. What first drew a man to the shelter of a woman and her children was not love but hunger for food.
p084.s1.b1: Maternal love, by contrast, is instinctive. It does not come from the mores but is bestowed by the adjutant mind-spirits of the local universe, and its strength is in proportion to the length of the species’ helpless infancy. This strong attachment drew woman into the protective enclosure of marriage and, at the same time, put her at a great disadvantage in her struggle with man.
p084.s1.b3: The home came into being when these temporary partnerships lasted long enough to rear the offspring. The author says that the co-operation of one man and one woman is in most respects far superior to that of two of the same sex, and that the pairing of the sexes improved survival and became the beginning of human society.
p084.s2.h: II–III. From the Mother-Family to the Father-Family
p084.s2.b0: Descent was at first reckoned only through the mother, because that was the only inheritance that was at all certain. In the mother-family the wife’s mother held the highest authority in the household, and the wife’s brothers were more involved in managing the family than the husband was. Then, when herding gave men control of the food supply, the mother-family quickly passed away.

p084.s2.b2: The author regards this change as one of the most radical about-faces the human race has ever made. Under father dominance the arbitrary authority of the father was the basis of family unity, and every society passed through a stage of patriarchal autocracy. The paper records calmly that woman’s low status came partly from the handicap of maternity, which kept her from being the hero of a crisis, and partly from her own exaltation of the warrior, which made her still more dependent.
p084.s2.b3: Yet woman was always the real producer. Her first liberation came when man consented to till the soil and began to use captives as agricultural laborers instead of killing them. The milk of cows and goats greatly reduced infant mortality, and when men brought to agriculture the organizational techniques they had learned in hunting and war, farming methods greatly improved.
p084.s3.h: IV–V. Woman’s Status — A Measure of Civilization
p084.s3.b1: The early woman was not a partner but a piece of property, and for a long time she was even regarded as having no soul. Taboos surrounding childbirth and menstruation made her unclean and dangerous. The author makes the folly of these ideas clear, yet also records the irony that the monthly seclusion gave overworked women a time of rest and meditation.

p084.s3.b4: The author does not see this as men deliberately seizing women’s rights and then grudgingly giving them back; it was all a process of unplanned social evolution. Tribes that persisted in cruelty to women did not survive. And it was not religion but science and industry that truly emancipated woman, so that evolution accomplished what even revelation had failed to do.
p084.s3.b6: The paper also sets the task that follows emancipation. How woman responds to her newly won recognition, dignity, and equality is the decisive test of the twentieth-century woman. Each sex has its own sphere and its own rights: woman cannot thrive on man’s rights, nor man on woman’s. Equality does not mean sameness.
p084.s4.h: VI. The Partnership of Man and Woman — A Complement That Endures
p084.s4.b0: Passion brings men and women together, but the weaker parental instinct and the social mores hold them together. Marriage is the highest manifestation of the antagonistic co-operation found where nature and society meet. The author frankly admits that man and woman are two distinct varieties of the same species, and that complete mutual understanding is impossible.

p084.s4.b3: This difference does not end with life on earth. The differing viewpoints of men and women continue through the morontia and spirit careers and into Havona, and even in the Corps of the Finality these personality trends are not erased. The two varieties will always intrigue, stimulate, and help each other. Hence the counsel to see the difference not as a concern but as a gift.
p084.s5.h: VII. The Ideals of Family Life — The First School of Brotherhood
p084.s5.b0: When the home is good, society is good. The cultural stability of the Jewish and Chinese peoples came from strong family groups. Marriage is now passing out of the property stage into the personal era, and as woman ceases to be property, new mores are emerging to stabilize marriage and the home.

4. The enhancement of parental instinct

p084.s5.b3: The large families of ancient times were wanted for reasons such as labor, security in old age, the extension of the family name, and fear of ghosts. Today’s ideal is different. Bringing a child into the world is not a parental right but carries the supreme responsibility of human existence; civilization regards the parents as assuming all duties and the child as having all the rights. A child’s respect grows not from the fact of being born but from care and training lovingly given.
p084.s5.b4: The paper’s observations on discipline are sharp as well. Ancient children learned early that disobedience meant failure or death, but civilization, by shielding children from the natural results of foolish conduct, sometimes fosters disobedience. The author names three factors that make modern child rearing difficult: a high degree of race mixture, artificial and superficial education, and parents absent so much that children cannot learn by watching and imitating them.
p084.s5.b6: The home is the basic unit of fraternity, where patience, altruism, tolerance, and forbearance are learned. The author recommends that families follow the Andite family council, which discussed everything freely and frankly, in place of patriarchal rule. And a good home, he says, shows children the first of a long series of disclosures of the love of the Paradise parent.
p084.s6.h: VIII. Dangers of Self-Gratification — The Pleasure Mania and the Home
p084.s6.b0: The greatest threat to family life is the modern pleasure mania. Property has served as the institution of self-maintenance, and marriage as the institution of self-perpetuation, but no distinct institution for self-gratification was ever established. As a result, the pursuit of pleasure permeates every institution, and even marriage is easily regarded merely as a means of pleasure.
p084.s6.b1: The play instinct and the sense of humor were new traits brought into human experience by the violet race, and the Adamic stock lifted them into new and glorified forms of self-gratification. But real danger arises when the restlessness, curiosity, and adventure of the post-Andite races combine with abandonment to pleasure. Even if every resource of art, color, and music is exhausted, these alone cannot elevate the soul or nourish the spirit, and vanity and fashion contribute nothing to home building.
p084.s6.b3: The author does not forbid enjoyment. Celestial beings too enjoy rest and the ministry of the reversion directors, and wholesome play, rest, and recreation all have value. Human beings are entitled to the full enjoyment of present joys. But if pleasure undermines property and destroys marriage and the home, it has been bought at a fatal price.
p084.s7.b0: Paper 84 portrays the family as man’s greatest purely human achievement. It began with the small nucleus of mother and child, passed through the antagonistic co-operation of man and woman, and became the place where children learn brotherhood and first glimpse the love of the Paradise parent. What guards this achievement is not the strength of institutions but the daily choice of parents to put responsibility before pleasure and service before rights.

p084.s7.b2: With the next paper, Paper 85, “The Origins of Worship,” attention turns from marriage and the home to how primitive religion began in the worship of natural objects and forces.
p085.lead: Stones and trees, animals and fire, sun and moon, and finally man himself: worship that began in fear and illusion, and under wisdom’s guidance turns to the God of nature.

p085.foot.text: Presented by a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon

p085.s0.h: Introduction — Primitive Religion Born of Fear and Illusion
p085.s0.b0: After three papers on marriage and the home, Paper 85 turns to the earliest roots of religion. Its author, a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon, says that primitive religion was a natural evolutionary development with a biologic origin, apart from moral associations and spiritual influences. Animals have fears too, but they have no religion because they have no illusions.
p085.s0.b2: The primitive manifestations of worship appeared long before any complex ideas of life here and hereafter. The objects of worship were things in nature that were near at hand or impressive. Man feared every manifestation of power he could not understand, and storms, floods, earthquakes, and volcanoes made a deep impression on his expanding mind. Only when religion rose above nature worship did it gain roots of spiritual origin.

p085.s1.h: I–II. Worship of Stones and Hills; Worship of Plants and Trees
p085.s1.b0: The first object evolving man worshiped was the stone. To someone who did not understand erosion, a stone that suddenly turned up in a field was a mystery, and a meteor streaking across the sky looked like the passage of a spirit. Jacob anointing a stone and Rachel hiding sacred stones belong to the long continuation of this awe. Stone worship was followed by hill worship: mountains became the dwelling places of good spirits and gods, and caves the entrances to the world of evil spirits.
p085.s1.b2: This sentence is also a caution against looking down on primitive people too easily. Simple mortals did not always identify the stone itself with Deity. Plants were at first feared and then worshiped because of the intoxicating liquors made from them, for intoxication was believed to make a person divine. Tree cults are among the oldest religious groups, and all early marriages were solemnized under trees.
p085.s1.b3: The nature of the spirit dwelling in a tree differed from people to people. The Finns believed most trees were occupied by kind spirits, the Swiss distrusted trees as harboring crafty spirits, and the peoples of India and eastern Russia regarded tree spirits as cruel. Except in China, there was once a universal cult of the tree of life. That people could imagine such different characters for the same object shows that the content of worship came more from the human mind than from the object.

p085.s1.b5: The author adds that even amid this jumble of nature worship, the earliest worship, activated by the adjutant mind-spirit, was already functioning long before man’s religious nature could respond fully to spiritual influences. However superstitious the surface, a stimulus from above was flowing beneath it.
p085.s2.h: III. The Worship of Animals — Symbol and Idol
p085.s2.b0: Primitive man felt a peculiar kinship with the higher animals and stood in awe of their strength and cunning. Every animal was at some time worshiped by some race, and half-human, half-animal beings such as centaurs and mermaids were worshiped as well. The Hebrews worshiped serpents down to the days of Hezekiah, the Chinese worship of the dragon is a relic of the serpent cult, and the wisdom of the serpent became the symbol of Greek medicine.
p085.s2.b1: The worship of insects and other animals was also promoted by a misapplication of the golden rule to every form of life. Animal symbols often point to forgotten gods or vanished cults. It was in this era too that the lamb became the sacrificial animal and the dove the symbol of peace and love.
p085.s2.b3: The author holds that a symbol may be good or bad depending on whether it displaces the original idea of worship. When a symbol such as a candle becomes a window that leads the mind to God, it helps; when it becomes an end in itself, it slides into idolatry. Believers today can examine their own symbols by this standard.
p085.s3.h: IV. Worship of the Elements — Water and Wind, Thunder and Fire
p085.s3.b0: Mankind has worshiped earth, air, water, and fire. Bubbling springs and rushing streams strongly suggested spiritual vitality, and sometimes a drowning person was not rescued for fear of offending the river god. Thunder was taken for the voice of an angry god, and fire worship reached its height in Persia. Belief in nature spirits was strong enough to survive into Hebrew theology in Moses’ day as angels of fire, water, and air.

p085.s3.b2: That the same phenomenon could be a blessing in one region and a curse in another shows that the objects of primitive religion were determined less by their own nature than by people’s living conditions and fears. The author also explains why magic survived so long.
p085.s3.b4: This observation still holds today. We remember the hunch that came true and quickly forget the ones that missed. Superstition grows on this selective memory even more than on ignorance. Honest faith begins with a mind that does not forget its failures.
p085.s4.h: V. Worship of the Heavenly Bodies — From Moon to Sun
p085.s4.b0: The worship of stones, trees, and animals passed through reverence for the elements to the deification of sun, moon, and stars. Moon worship reached its height in the hunting era, and sun worship became the chief rite of the agricultural age. Sun worship first took root in India and lasted longest there; in Persia it gave rise to the Mithraic cult, and later civilizations named the first day of the week after the sun. In India and elsewhere the stars were thought of as the glorified souls of great men who had left the life of the flesh, and the Chaldean star cultists regarded themselves as children of the sky father and the earth mother.
p085.s4.b1: The sun-god was regarded as the mystic father of virgin-born sons of destiny. These babies were believed to be set adrift on some sacred river, miraculously rescued, and to grow up to become deliverers of their people. The author records plainly that such savior traditions grew out of the worship of the heavenly bodies.
p085.s5.h: VI. Worship of Man — Gods in Human Form
p085.s5.b0: Having worshiped everything on earth and in the sky, man at last worshiped himself. The savage made no clear distinction between beasts, men, and gods. Extraordinary persons were regarded as superhuman, those with mental disorders as indwelt by a god, and priests, kings, and prophets were worshiped too. Dead chiefs were deified, and in later times distinguished souls were sainted.
p085.s5.b1: The author says that unaided evolution never produced gods higher than the glorified spirits of deceased humans. Man worship reached its peak when rulers demanded veneration from their subjects and claimed descent from the gods. This is also an old warning that religion can become a tool of power.
p085.s5.b2: The ghost gods that arose from human beings must be distinguished from the nature gods, nature spirits elevated to the status of deity. The nature cult and the later ghost cult developed side by side and influenced each other, and many religious systems embraced both concepts. Sometimes the two were intertwined in a single god, as in Thor, a ghost hero who was also master of the lightning.

p085.s6.h: VII. The Adjutants of Worship and Wisdom
p085.s6.b0: Nature worship seemed to arise spontaneously in the minds of primitive men, and in a sense it did. Yet all along the sixth adjutant, the spirit of worship, was constantly stimulating the human urge to worship. Animal fear may have triggered worship and its objects may have been natural things, but the worship urge itself had a definite origin.

head: Adjutant spirit
Its ministry
How it appears in worship
rows: Sixth: the spirit of worship

Seventh: the spirit of wisdom

p085.s6.b4: The author asks us to remember that feeling, not thinking, dominated all evolutionary development. The desire to worship was there from the beginning, but what it turned toward changed as wisdom grew. The maturing of worship, then, does not lie in discarding feeling but in letting feeling be guided by thought born of meditation and experience. When awe grows beyond fear into understanding of the Creator, primitive worship becomes real religion.
p085.s7.b0: Paper 85 is a catalog of the things mankind has worshiped, and at the same time a testimony that the urge to worship was planted in man from the beginning. Mingled with fear and illusion, that urge turned to stones, trees, and animals, but when wisdom guides it, it turns from nature to the Creator of nature. Relics that survive today, such as the Maypole and the Christmas tree, candles and tombstones, are footprints of that long journey.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Worship out of love and wisdom, not fear
Real religion is the worship urge directed by wisdom
Watch that symbols do not become ends in themselves
Symbolism must not be confused with idolatry
Remember honestly the results that missed
The devotee of magic nonchalantly forgets his failures
Do not exalt people or leaders as gods
Man worship peaked in the deification of rulers
Look through nature’s beauty to its Creator
Worship turns from nature to the God of nature

p085.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 86, “Early Evolution of Religion,” goes on to show how this worship urge, amid fear of luck and misfortune, dreams and death, grew into the ideas of ghosts and spirits.
p086.lead: Good luck and bad, the shock of death, and the ghost idea born of dreams and breath: primitive religion that grew up in fear and in the end prepared the way for ethics and the Adjuster’s bestowal.

p086.foot.text: Presented by an Evening Star of Nebadon

p086.s0.h: Introduction — Religion That Grows Without Revelation
p086.s0.b0: Following the nature worship of the previous paper, Paper 86 looks at the experiences through which primitive religion took shape. Its author, an Evening Star of Nebadon, explains that man’s prereligious fear of natural forces became religious as nature was personalized, spiritized, and finally deified in human consciousness.
p086.s0.b2: The normal functioning of the human mind under the guidance of the sixth and seventh mind-adjutants is quite enough to ensure this development. The paper follows four experiences that drove the process—chance and bad luck, the mystery of death, dreams and breath, and an imagined ghost environment—and shows what all of them finally prepared the way for.
p086.s1.h: I–II. Chance and Its Personification — The Religion of Good and Bad Luck
p086.s1.b0: The results of the hunt always varied, and for primitive people living on the edge of survival, bad luck was a great factor. They struggled not for a standard of living but for existence itself, and dread of unseen calamity overshadowed every joy. Even a run of good luck was feared as a sign of coming disaster. Caught between the desire to get something for nothing and the fear of getting nothing for something, existence itself was a gamble.
p086.s1.b2: Herders inherited the same outlook, and farmers were even more keenly aware that their crops depended on things beyond their control, such as drought and flood, hail and insects. These ideas permeated the philosophy of all ancient peoples and survived in the confession that the race is not always to the swift, and that time and chance happen to all. The gambling tendency that remains among partially civilized peoples today is a trace of this ancient experience.
p086.s1.b3: Unable to find a material cause, primitive man asked, “Who is doing this to me?” and found his answer in spirits. So religion was born of fear of the mysterious and awe of the unseen. His mind was logical but short of ideas; when one event followed another, he took it as cause and effect. What civilized man calls superstition was for the savage simply the result of ignorance.
p086.s1.b5: The author points out that to keep ascribing hard-to-understand things to supernatural causes is a lazy way of avoiding intellectual hard work. Words like luck and chance describe a state of being too ignorant or too indolent to determine causes. But as exploration continues, the belief in chance breaks down, and in its place comes a universe of law and order in which every effect is preceded by a definite cause.
p086.s1.b7: The author also says that when anxiety becomes pain, activity is inhibited and evolutionary change follows; pain and suffering are essential to progressive evolution. He adds that not all religion grew out of animism. Other concepts of the supernatural existed at the same time, and they too led to worship.
p086.s2.h: III–IV. Death, and Survival Beyond Death
p086.s2.b1: Among savages, death usually came by violence, so nonviolent death was all the more mysterious. It took ages for the idea of death as the natural end of life to take hold. At first all sickness and natural death were believed to be caused by spirit influence, and even later, complex theologies attributed death to the action of the spirit world, giving rise to doctrines such as original sin and the fall.
p086.s2.b2: The idea of survival after death was born of the chance association of everyday events with ghost dreams. When several tribesmen dreamed of a dead chief on the same night, it seemed proof that he had returned. Breath, visible as a cloud on a cold day, was the sign that divided the living from the dead, and the breath without a body became the spirit, the ghost. This dream-ghost-future-life idea began to serve as an antidote to the fear of death.

head: People
Their idea of the destiny of the dead
rows: The Greeks
Weak men have weak souls, which go to Hades
The early Andites
Ghosts return to the ancestral homelands
The Chinese and Egyptians
Soul and body remain together, leading to tomb building and body preservation
The Hebrews
A phantom replica goes down to Sheol and cannot return
The orange race
A strong belief in transmigration and reincarnation

p086.s2.b4: The primitive doctrine of survival did not mean immortality. People who could not count beyond twenty could not grasp eternity, so they imagined repeated reincarnations. At first there was no idea of hell or future punishment; the next life was thought of as something like this one without bad luck. The paper notes that the belief that a person dies three to seven times preserves a remnant of Adam’s teaching about the mansion worlds, showing that traces of revelation are mixed even into evolutionary religion.
p086.s3.h: V. The Ghost-Soul Concept — The Other Self of Dreams
p086.s3.b0: The soul was first thought of as the dream self, exactly like oneself except that it could not be touched. This belief spread to the idea that all things, living and nonliving, had souls, and it long sustained belief in nature spirits. The soul was thought to be related to the body as perfume to a flower, and it was believed able to leave the body in various ways.

head: When the soul leaves the body
Related customs and beliefs
rows: 1. Ordinary transient fainting
The soul has moved away for a moment
2. Sleep and dreams
Sleepers were awakened slowly so the soul had time to return
3. Coma and unconsciousness
A sign of death, the soul trying to leave for good
4. Death
Permanent departure, “giving up the ghost”
Sneezing
A failed attempt of the soul to escape, followed by a blessing

p086.s3.b2: There were many beliefs about where the soul resided: in the breath, the shadow, the head, the hair, the heart, the liver, the blood, or the fat. From these came customs such as turning mirrors to the wall, the taboo against eating fat, and the expression calling the eyes the windows of the soul. The descendants of Badonan believed in two souls, the breath and the shadow, and the Greeks in three: vegetative, animal, and intellectual.
p086.s3.b3: Because the soul was thought to pass with the breath, a brave chief would breathe into a newborn child to impart courage, and an eldest son would try to catch his dying father’s last breath. The idea that a soul could enter an animal spread into the belief in werewolves. Those who believed in several souls held that losing one meant discomfort, two meant illness, and three meant death, and the shaman was thought to perform a “new birth” by exchanging a sick soul for a new one.
p086.s3.b4: The Hebrews believed that God spoke in dreams, and Moses forbade the belief; the author says Moses was right, because ordinary dreams are not the method by which personalities of the spiritual world communicate with material beings. As civilization advances, man comes to depend on revelation and personal religious experience for a new concept of the soul: the soul as the joint creation of the God-knowing mortal mind and the indwelling Thought Adjuster.
p086.s4.h: VI. The Ghost-Spirit Environment — The Birth of Right and Wrong
p086.s4.b0: Man inherited a natural environment, acquired a social environment, and imagined a ghost environment. When this imagined spirit world was accepted as real, the mind and moral life of mankind were changed forever. Until the age of revelation this was the only religion man had, and many races today still have only this crude evolutionary religion.

head: Environment
How it was obtained
The institution that arose in response
rows: Natural environment
Inherited
The state
Social environment
Acquired
The home
Ghost environment
Imagined
The church

p086.s4.b3: This sentence teaches humility. Among the ideas we are sure of today, some will be errors at which later generations smile. Yet this age of superstition bore an unexpected fruit. Once people believed that angry spirits brought bad luck and pleased spirits good luck, they had to adjust their conduct accordingly, and with that the idea of right and wrong was born. The long and wasteful effort spent on tombs, temples, sacrifices, and priesthoods was a terrible price, but it was worth what it cost.
p086.s5.h: VII. The Function of Primitive Religion — From Insurance to Philosophy
p086.s5.b0: The savage insured himself against bad luck by paying costly premiums of fear, superstition, and gifts to priests. Primitive religion was the payment of premiums against the perils of the forest. Modern society has moved this function from religion to economics, and actuaries have replaced the capricious gods. As a result, religion is moving away from being a system of insurance against bad luck and rising to higher philosophic levels.

head: Aspect
Primitive man
Modern man
rows: Dangers insured against
The perils of the forest, bad luck
Industrial accidents, the hazards of modern life
Premiums paid
Fear, superstition, dread, gifts to priests
Material premiums
Who calculates
Fictitious spirits and capricious gods
Actuaries using mathematics
Religion’s concern
Controlling luck
Life beyond the grave, higher philosophic levels

p086.s5.b2: Even so, ancient religion kept people from falling into fatalism or hopeless pessimism, because they believed they could do something to change their fate. The author also leaves a warning for modern people: while giving up the error of blaming bad luck on spirits, they are accepting an almost equally false idea that attributes all inequality to political, social, and industrial causes alone. Legislation and philanthropy are good, but they will not remedy the facts of birth and the accidents of living.
p086.s5.b4: The last paragraph of the paper gives meaning to the whole long story. By the force of false fear, primitive religion plowed the soil of the human mind and prepared it for the bestowal of a true spiritual force of supernatural origin, the Thought Adjuster. Ever since, the Adjusters have labored to transmute God-fear into God-love.
p086.s6.b0: Paper 86 does not hide that religion’s beginnings were not beautiful. Religion grew out of fear of bad luck, the shock of death, and the illusions of dreams. Yet from that rough soil a sense of right and wrong sprouted, and a place was prepared for the Adjuster to dwell. The task left to us is to complete a religion that began in fear as a religion of love, and that is the very work the Adjuster is already doing within us.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it

The word chance covers ignorance or indolence

Hold even your present certainties with humility
Each generation repeats errors that posterity will smile at
Do not blame every inequality on others
Comprehension of facts and wise action are the antidote
Turn a faith of fear into a faith of love
The Adjusters transmute God-fear into God-love

p086.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 87, “The Ghost Cults,” continues the story, showing how the ghost idea developed into ghost fear and placation, ancestor worship and exorcism, and finally ceremonialism.
p087.lead: How a religion of insurance, born of fear of the dead, grew through ancestor worship and the dualism of good and evil spirits into ritual and symbol.

p087.foot.text: Presented by a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon

p087.s0.h: Introduction — Born of Fear, Not Reverence
p087.s0.b0: Paper 87 examines how the ghost idea discussed in the previous paper hardened into a cult. Its author, a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon, says that primitive religious observances arose not from reverence for Deity but from anxiety about bad luck and an inordinate fear of the dead. Their rites were mostly negative, designed to avoid, expel, or coerce ghosts.
p087.s0.b2: The author says that nothing is more pitiful than the sight of man in bondage to ghost-spirit fear, yet he holds that this very fear set mankind on the road of religious evolution. His remark that human imagination, having left the shores of self, will not find its anchorage until it arrives at the concept of a true Deity invites us to read the whole paper as the starting point of a long voyage.
p087.s1.h: I–II. Ghost Fear and Ghost Placation — The Roots of Funeral Customs
p087.s1.b0: To primitive man, death meant that one more ghost had been released from a body. Ghosts were thought to have supernatural power but no intelligence, so people used all kinds of tricks to deceive them. A house where someone had died was torn down or abandoned, and this fear delayed the appearance of solid houses and permanent villages.

head: Custom
Its original motive
rows: Carrying the body out through a hole in the wall
Confusing the ghost so it could not return
Returning from the burial by another road
Keeping the ghost from following
Men and women exchanging clothes; mourning dress
First a disguise for the survivors, later respect and placation
Keeping a light and watching beside the body
Fear of leaving it in darkness
The funeral sermon
Instructing the new ghost on the way to the land of the dead
Leaving food and clothing at the grave
Provision for the ghost’s journey
Not speaking the name of the dead
The name became taboo, impoverishing language

p087.s1.b2: The first acts of human worship were defensive. Just as people today insure against fire, the savage thought it wise to insure against the bad luck ghosts might bring. Because ghosts had to be quickly “laid” and sent off to the land of the dead, people feared that even a small mistake in the ritual could bring disaster from an angry ghost.
p087.s1.b4: This fear exacted a high price. Self-mutilation in mourning, unproductive mourning that consumed weeks or months every year, and hired professional mourners all show that mourning was a ritual, not grief. Believing that ghosts wanted their wives and servants, people buried or killed them along with the dead, and broke or burned tools and property. Civilization took a great step forward when inheritance by relatives replaced the burning and burying of property, and the Iroquois, who reformed funeral waste, became the most powerful of the northern red men.
p087.s1.b6: The belief that ghosts enjoyed the smell of food made funeral food offerings universal, and throwing a little food into the fire before a meal while muttering a formula was primitive man’s way of praying. Compared with today’s grace at the table, it suggests how far the same gesture has traveled, from fear to gratitude.
p087.s2.h: III–IV. Ancestor Worship; Good and Bad Spirit Ghosts — The Gains and Costs of Dualism
p087.s2.b0: The ghost cult inevitably led to ancestor worship, which became the link between common ghosts and the higher spirits, the evolving gods. Adopting children was a way to make sure someone would make offerings for one’s soul after death, and the Romans held twelve ghost feasts a year.
p087.s2.b2: At first people believed in only one kind of ghost, which brought good luck when pleased and bad luck when angered. Later they imagined spirits that had advanced beyond ghostland to higher realms, and finally the dual spiritism of good and bad spirits arose independently all over the world. The author observes that the power of an idea over the mind lies not in its reality but in its vividness and the ease of its application.

head: Aspect
Single spiritism
Dual spiritism
rows: Kinds of spirits
One kind of ghost
Good spirits and bad spirits
Character of the spirits
Wholly capricious
Somewhat consistent behavior
What was gained
An explanation of both good and bad luck; the idea of consistent supermortal forces
What it cost
Cosmic unity became hard to conceive; the gods were set against the forces of darkness

p087.s2.b4: Dualism was a great advance in religious philosophy, but it was also a heavy burden. The idea of good and evil as cosmic equals has survived into the twentieth century, and the author says that most of the world’s religions still carry this cultural birthmark of the age of the ghost cults.
p087.s3.h: V. The Advancing Ghost Cult — Envious Spirits and Prosperity Insurance
p087.s3.b0: Primitive man believed that spirits had only rights and no duties, and that men had only duties and no rights. Even the smallest misfortune was blamed on ghosts, and after making offerings to every known spirit, people still did not feel safe, so they made one more to “the unknown gods.” Religious organization developed as a self-adjustment to the spirit environment, just as industry was an adjustment to nature and marriage to the demands of bisexuality.
p087.s3.b2: Good spirits were neglected on the assumption that they would do their work anyway, while great effort went into keeping bad spirits pleased. Prosperity in particular was thought to arouse the envy of spirits, and fear of the evil eye spread almost world-wide. People disclaimed praise and gave themselves ugly names; this custom was later refined into courtesy and modesty, but for a long time it hindered the development of art.

head: The new world philosophy
Its content
rows: 1. Duty
The things that keep the spirits favorable, or at least neutral
2. Right
The correct conduct and ceremonies that win the spirits over to one’s interests
3. Truth
The right understanding of and attitude toward spirits, and so toward life and death

p087.s3.b5: Under this system life became a gamble that depended on the favor of spirits rather than on effort and talent. People tried to discover the will of the spirits through omens, dreams, and divination, not out of curiosity but in a struggle to dodge bad luck. The author points out that remnants of these superstitions linger even among civilized races.
p087.s4.h: VI. Coercion and Exorcism — From Placating to Commanding
p087.s4.b0: Once the idea of good and bad spirits took hold, religion moved beyond the negative stage of bribing spirits to avert bad luck to a positive stage of trying to compel their co-operation. To make up for his helplessness before forces he could not control, man looked for techniques to even the odds in his one-sided struggle with the cosmos.

head: No.
Techniques for frightening and driving away ghosts
rows: Cutting off the head and burying the body tied up
Stoning the house of the dead
Castrating the corpse or breaking its legs
Burying under stones, one origin of the modern tombstone
Cremation, a later invention to prevent ghost trouble
Casting the body into the sea
Exposing the body to wild animals

p087.s4.b2: Noise, foul smells, frightening images, and above all water became means of keeping ghosts away. The custom of circling the corpse with water led to holy water, and in primitive times bathing was a religious ceremony rather than a matter of hygiene. Exorcism was the use of one spirit to control another, and vows and oaths, fasting and self-denial were also regarded as ways to compel reluctant spirits, becoming the roots of asceticism.
p087.s4.b4: The observation that knocking on wood, crossing one’s fingers, and the archaic style reserved for prayer come from the same roots invites readers to look at their own religious habits. It asks whether our relationship with God is turning into a bargain or an incantation.
p087.s5.h: VII. Nature of Cultism — Symbols Must Grow
p087.s5.b0: The cult has endured because it provided symbols that preserve and stimulate moral sentiment and religious loyalty. Yet while the cult guards feeling, it has also been the greatest obstacle to social reconstruction and spiritual progress. The author regrets that so many modern believers in moral ideals have no adequate symbolism to share and lean on together.
p087.s5.b2: When the cult was flexible and its symbols could expand, truth grew and spread rapidly. On the other hand, a cult that has lost its meaning degrades religion when it tries to take the place of philosophy or to enslave reason. Modern man is collectively scientific and averse to superstition but individually hungry for mystery, so a surviving symbolism must be one the individual can practice for himself and also share with others.
p087.s5.b3: The author judges that the early Christian cult was the most effective and enduring ritual ever devised, but that in the scientific age it has weakened as many of its fundamental tenets were lost. Every new revelation of truth has given rise to a new cult, and when the religion of Jesus is restated, new symbols expressing the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man must grow as well.

Dynamism

p087.s6.b0: Paper 87 does not hide how low a place religion started from: fear and self-defense. Yet the story does not end in cynicism. The same fear sent mankind out on a voyage in search of a true God, and the cult appears not as something to discard but as a skeleton that must grow anew to support living spiritual experience. The task this paper leaves us is to check whether remnants of the ghost cult still linger in our own faith.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Make faith an investment in growth, not insurance against bad luck

Lay down the habit of bargaining with God

Do not see good and evil as equal cosmic forces

Remember the dead with respect and love, not fear
The ancients mourned because of fear
Let rites and symbols grow out of love put into practice
The new cult must be the outgrowth of applied love

p087.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 88, “Fetishes, Charms, and Magic,” continues the story of coercion and exorcism, showing how the belief that spirits dwell in objects and persons led to fetishes and magic.
p088.lead: How the belief that spirits dwell in objects and persons grew into fetishes and totems, magic and charms, and finally became the cocoon that held science.

p088.foot.text: Presented by a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon

p088.s0.h: Introduction — Not the Object, but the Spirit Within
p088.s0.b0: Following the paper on the ghost cults, Paper 88 examines the very ancient belief that a spirit can enter an inanimate object, an animal, or a human being. Its author, a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon, defines this doctrine of spirit possession as fetishism. At first the fetish was thought to be inhabited by the ghost of a dead person; later, higher spirits were believed to reside in it.
p088.s0.b2: This perspective keeps us from treating fetishism as simple foolishness. The urge to tie an unseen power to something visible had its own logic for primitive man, and that logic bound together all his early ideas of ghosts, souls, spirits, and demon possession. The paper patiently traces the forms in which that logic survives today.
p088.s1.h: I. Belief in Fetishes — Anything Unusual Became a Fetish
p088.s1.b0: Primitive man made a fetish of anything out of the ordinary. If he fell ill and chanced to recover, the object he carried at the time became a fetish; so did objects connected with dreams. Volcanoes became fetishes but mountains did not; comets did, but stars did not. Unusualness, together with chance, made fetishes.
p088.s1.b1: Animals were especially frequent fetishes. An animal that had eaten human flesh could become one, and when a ghost was believed to dwell permanently in a fetish animal, fetishism could shade into the idea of reincarnation. The savage envied animals and did not feel superior to them, and he often named himself after his favorite beast.

head: What became a fetish
Examples and their traces
rows: Stones
Stones with peculiar markings, the first fetishes; bead necklaces; “sacred stones”
Fire and water
Surviving in fire worship and belief in holy water
Plants and fruits
Taboo as food once they became fetishes, such as the apple
Animals
Eating their flesh was taboo: apes, serpents, cattle, and others
Days and numbers
Unlucky Friday and thirteen; four, the lucky number of primitive man
Parts of the body
Spittle, hair, nails, skulls, the navel cord
Unusual persons
The crippled, the insane, epileptics, geniuses: fetish personalities

p088.s1.b3: The most consequential practice was making fetishes of human beings. A genius was thought to be a fetish personality indwelt by a wise spirit, and such persons soon began to resort to fraud and trickery for their own advantage. From the fetish person, revered as more than human and even infallible, grew the unlimited authority of chiefs, kings, priests, and church rulers.
p088.s1.b4: Other details are striking as well: the ancients opposed taking a census because counting livestock or property was thought to bring bad luck, and primitive man did not make an undue fetish of sex and was not obscene. Superstitions stay with us longer than we think, and we should not be quick to look down on primitive people.
p088.s2.h: II. Evolution of the Fetish — From Relics to Words
p088.s2.b0: Ghosts were believed to prefer to dwell in objects they had owned in life, and this belief led to the veneration of relics and to pilgrimages to the tombs of great men. The author sees the relics of modern religions as an attempt to rationalize the savage’s fetish and raise it to a place of dignity.
p088.s2.b1: The hearth of the home became a sacred place, and shrines and temples became fetish places because they were at first burial places of the dead. The author relates that Moses exalted the Hebrew fetish hut into the place that housed a superfetish, the law of God, yet the Israelites never gave up the Canaanite belief that the spirit of God dwelt in stone altars.
p088.s2.b3: Images and idols were an elaborate form of fetishism. Moses tried to check fetish worship by adding the second commandment against graven images, and in his wisdom he did not sweep away the old fetishes all at once but had certain relics kept in the ark together with the law. But even that commandment later became a supreme fetish, used to stifle art and the enjoyment of beauty.

head: Stage
The form of the fetish
rows: A chief’s nail parings, sacred stones
Bones and relics of the dead; shrines and temples that were once burial places
Images and idols, at first memorials, believed indwelt by spirit through consecration
Words and writings regarded as inspired: sacred books
The authority of churches, founded on accepting the authority of those writings

p088.s2.b6: The author warns against believing that everything in a book is true and that all truth is contained in it. Opening the book at random to let it decide one’s life, or swearing with a hand on the book, are forms of refined fetishism. Yet he fairly acknowledges that moving from fear of a chief’s nail parings to reverence for a collection of the moral wisdom of centuries is real progress.
p088.s3.h: III. Totemism — From Clan God to National Flag
p088.s3.b0: Fetishism ran through every primitive cult, from sacred stones through idolatry and nature worship to totemism. Totemism combined social and religious observances: the totem was at once the symbol of the group and its god, the clan personified. The author regards it as one phase of the attempt to socialize an otherwise personal religion.
p088.s3.b2: Just as the medicine man never let his medicine bag touch the ground, people today take care that the flag does not touch the ground. The fetish of the supreme state evolved from clan to tribe, from suzerainty to sovereignty, from totem to flag. The author observes that man has even made a fetish of democracy: he takes lightly the ordinary thinking of one person, yet when it is gathered into “public opinion,” he honors it as the standard of justice.
p088.s3.b3: The story of the totem does not condemn symbols as such. A symbol that binds a group together served its purpose as a stage of socialization. The trouble begins when the symbol is raised above the values it points to and is revered for its own sake, like the insignia of priesthood and kingship. The fetish kings who ruled by “divine right” are an example.
p088.s4.h: IV–V. Magic and Magical Charms — Techniques for an Illusory Spirit World

head: Aspect
Magic
Science
rows: The environment it deals with
The conjectured spirit environment
The real environment
Aims
To foresee the future and influence the environment favorably
The same two aims
How it was reached
Long experience and painful failure
Experiment and method
When it fails
The cure is more magic
It steadily reduces the gambling element in life

p088.s4.b2: Mankind moved from magic to science not through meditation and reason but through long experience. As the author puts it, man backed into the truth and only faced forward once the scientific method arrived. The fear and curiosity in superstition were the first expressions of the desire to understand and control the planetary environment.
p088.s4.b4: Because natural death was not understood, magic held the savage in a powerful grip. Ten innocent people might be executed for a single natural death, and fear itself could kill, which only confirmed the false belief. Hair and nails, spittle and food scraps were hidden or buried for fear an enemy would use them for sorcery, so even habits that look like hygiene actually came from fear.
p088.s4.b5: Charms were made from all sorts of things, from tiger claws and crocodile teeth to snake venom, bones of the dead, and dust from footprints. People believed that mistreating or honoring an image would affect the real person it represented. Notice that the customs of new or higher civilizations were suspected of being evil magic and shunned; writing, printing, and pictures were long treated this way. The fear that labels the unfamiliar as magic is an old habit that slows progress.
p088.s4.b7: Names too were objects of magic. A name was regarded as a precious entity, like the soul or the shadow, and could even be pawned; the real name was not told to strangers, and so nicknames arose. The author sees a trace of this in people today signing promissory notes and striving for titles and degrees.
p088.s5.h: VI. The Practice of Magic — From Incantation to Prayer, From Magic to Science
p088.s5.b0: There was public magic and private magic. The magic of medicine men, shamans, and priests was thought to serve the welfare of the whole tribe, while the magic of witches and sorcerers was private and selfish, aimed at harming enemies. Here the dualism of good and bad spirits led to the belief in white and black magic.
p088.s5.b1: In magic, “medicine” meant not healing but mystery. The savage did not treat himself and never used remedies without the advice of a magic expert. The paper also records that among primitive magicians there were more women than men.
p088.s5.b2: Some chants and incantations eventually evolved into prayers. Prayers were also acted out; magical dances were dramatic prayers. Gestures, being older than words, were considered more sacred, and imitation, as in the buffalo dance, was believed to have great power.

p088.s5.b5: Yet a world full of charms crushed individual ambition and initiative. A man whose harvest exceeded his neighbor’s was suspected of luring grain from the other’s field, and knowing too much risked being branded a black magician. The author warns that if education fails, people will promptly return to belief in magic, and he points to the linguistic fossils that remain in our speech as evidence.
p088.s6.b0: Paper 88 does not mock fetishes and magic so much as show how they have changed shape and survived in today’s relics and veneration of scripture, flags and public opinion, and belief in luck and astrology. The author observes that Urantia is in the twilight zone of intellectual evolution: half the world reaches for the light of truth and science, while the other half lies in the arms of thinly disguised magic. The reader is led to ask which half is larger within himself or herself.
p088.s6.b1: Nor does the paper simply praise science. Magic was a branch of the tree of evolutionary religion that bore the fruit of a scientific age, and prayer grew from the same root and displaced magic. Laying aside fear and facing reality honestly is the road that science and true religion travel together.

p088.s6.b3: The next paper, Paper 89, “Sin, Sacrifice, and Atonement,” continues the story of primitive religion, treating taboo and the idea of sin and the way the system of sacrifice was transformed into the sacraments.
p089.lead: From the fear of owing a debt to the spirits came taboo and sin, sacrifice and atonement—a long road through covenant and sacrament to sin understood as disloyalty.

p089.foot.text: Presented by a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon

p089.s0.h: Introduction — Man in Debt to the Spirits
p089.s0.b0: Paper 89 traces how primitive religion developed its ideas of sin and sacrifice. According to its author, a Brilliant Evening Star of Nebadon, primitive man regarded himself as being in debt to the spirits and in need of redemption. Over time this notion grew into a doctrine of sin and salvation: the soul was thought to come into the world under forfeit—original sin—and so had to be ransomed.
p089.s0.b1: The savage believed that the spirits took satisfaction in the sight of human misery and humiliation. At first he worried only about sins he had committed; later he became anxious about the things he had failed to do as well, and the whole sacrificial system grew up around these two ideas. The rituals of avoidance and exorcism, of coercion and propitiation, all blended into one another.
p089.s1.h: I. The Taboo — The First Social Regulation
p089.s1.b0: A taboo was the avoidance of some act in order to dodge ill luck and keep from offending the spirit ghosts. Taboos were not religious at first, but once they gained the sanction of ghosts and spirits, they became lawmakers and institution builders. The respect a taboo commanded exactly equaled the savage’s fear of the powers believed to enforce it; a man who broke one sometimes died of sheer fright.

p089.s1.b3: The later commandments were truly emancipating, because they replaced thousands of older taboos, and they definitely promised something in return for obedience. Taboos were highly effective in organizing society, yet they were also a terrible burden, preserving obsolete and useless bans alongside useful ones. Even so, the author judges that these achievements of self-control were the real rungs on which mankind climbed the ladder of civilization.
p089.s2.h: II. The Concept of Sin — Breaking the Taboo
p089.s2.b0: Every primitive tribe had its tree of forbidden fruit—literally the apple, but figuratively a tree whose thousand branches hung heavy with all sorts of taboos—and that tree always said, “⟦Q 89:2.1⟧Thou shalt not.⟦/Q⟧” Once the savage mind could imagine both good and bad spirits, and once taboo received the sanction of evolving religion, the stage was set for the idea of sin. That idea was universal long before revealed religion appeared.
p089.s2.b2: Sin in this sense was an act, not a thought; a matter of ritual, not of reason. The traditions of Dilmun and Eden reinforced the belief that man began in perfection and fell through breaking taboos. Habitual violation became a vice; primitive law made vice a crime, and religion made it a sin. The remark that hells had to be invented to explain the prosperity of the wicked shows what ideas people devised in their longing for justice.
p089.s2.b3: Confession and forgiveness appeared early too, but confession was merely a rite of remission—men would even ask forgiveness for sins they intended to commit the following week—and a public announcement of defilement. Many apparently hygienic customs were in fact largely ceremonial.
p089.s3.h: III. Renunciation and Humiliation — From Self-Denial to Self-Control
p089.s3.b0: Renunciation was the next step. Fasting and the giving up of pleasures became customary; property came to be seen as a spiritual handicap, and tens of thousands of earnest souls began to court poverty. Flogging and the mortification of the flesh were regarded as ways of earning extra credit on the gods’ ledgers. Yet the author holds that all this taught the savage self-control.
p089.s3.b1: Self-denial and self-control were two of the greatest social gains of early evolutionary religion. Man learned to enlarge life’s fraction by lowering the denominator of personal demands rather than always trying to raise the numerator of selfish gratification. The continence cult, on the other hand, tolerated marriage only as a lesser evil than fornication. The author explains that the Apostle Paul’s personal views on celibacy reflected this cult, and that Paul himself knew such teachings were not part of Jesus’ gospel, saying he spoke “⟦Q 89:3.6⟧by permission and not by commandment.⟦/Q⟧”
p089.s3.b3: The counsel that someday man should learn to enjoy liberty without license, nourishment without gluttony, and pleasure without debauchery offers today’s reader a standard of balance. So does the warning that the continence cult leads to a war against marriage and the home, society’s veritable foundation.
p089.s4.h: IV. Origins of Sacrifice — Gift, Debt, and Substitution
p089.s4.b0: The tendency to bow before power is foreshadowed in the fawning of a dog before its master, and from the impulse of worship to the act of sacrifice was but one step. Primitive man measured the value of a sacrifice by the pain it cost him, so the first sacrifices were such acts as plucking hair, cutting the flesh, and cutting off fingers.

p089.s4.b2: Sacrifice came to be thought of as a message bearer to the gods, and incense and other aesthetic features were added; rites of conciliation and propitiation replaced the older methods of avoidance and exorcism. The doctrine of original sin started every person out in serious debt to the spirit powers. If renunciation was the negative form of propitiation, sacrifice became its positive form.
p089.s4.b4: The staggering list of offerings claimed by a certain Egyptian ruler suggests how heavily such sacrifices must have taxed his toiling subjects. In the end, sheer necessity drove people to eat the material part of their sacrifices, the gods having enjoyed the soul of it, and the custom was justified as a sacred meal.
p089.s5.h: V–VI. Sacrifices and Cannibalism; Evolution of Human Sacrifice — An Honest Record of a Dark Past
p089.s5.b0: The author says that modern ideas of early cannibalism are entirely wrong. It arose from necessity and persisted through superstition and ignorance; it was a social, economic, religious, and military custom of early society. Because ghost spirits were thought to be merely modified men, whose greatest need must be food, human flesh was offered to them. The Andonites, Nodites, and Adamites were originally not cannibals.

p089.s5.b3: Human sacrifice was virtually universal; no race has been entirely free of it. The Chaldeans were among the first to substitute animals, and a tenderhearted Japanese emperor introduced clay images in place of human victims. The author calls the Hebrew story of Jephthah, who sacrificed his only daughter because of a foolish vow, the most tragic record of the clash between time-honored custom and advancing civilization. He adds that the story of Abraham and Isaac was not a strange idea to the people of that day.
p089.s5.b4: The “foundation sacrifice,” in which a person was slain when an important new building was begun, survives in the modern custom of placing keepsakes in a cornerstone. The contrast between “⟦Q 89:6.7⟧life for life⟦/Q⟧,” once spoken at sacrifice, and “⟦Q 89:6.7⟧dust to dust⟦/Q⟧,” now spoken at death, shows how far ritual has traveled.
p089.s6.h: VII–VIII. Modifications of Human Sacrifice; Redemption and Covenants — From Bargain to Trust
p089.s6.b0: Moses tried to end human sacrifice by setting up a system of ransom, under which lands, properties, and children could be redeemed for fixed fees. Groups that stopped sacrificing their first-born soon held great advantages over neighbors who lost sons and saw even their succession of leadership broken. Human sacrifice changed form many times: blood smeared on doorposts, infants set adrift on the water, exile and colonization, temple prostitution, vows of virginity, and the offering of parts of the body.
p089.s6.b1: In time sacrifice became linked with the idea of the covenant. Man could not imagine a dependable God until he himself had become relatively dependable and moral, so the thought of making a covenant with Deity was evidence of growing moral dignity. Still, the author warns us not to mistake these early sacrifices for spontaneous gifts of gratitude; they were not expressions of true worship.
p089.s6.b3: Early prayer, too, was bargaining with the spirits and argument with the gods. As commerce developed, the spirit of trade entered worship, and just as some men were better traders, some were thought better at praying. The observation that prayers are still read from books, recited by rote, and hung on wheels and trees for the wind to say invites us to ask how much our own praying has really changed.
p089.s7.h: IX–X. Sacrifices and Sacraments; Forgiveness of Sin — Loyalty Restored
p089.s7.b0: Human sacrifice advanced from the bloody business of man-eating to higher and more symbolic levels, and the early rituals of sacrifice bred the later sacraments. A sacrament of cakes and wine took the place of the flesh and blood of human sacrifice, and from the Hebrew Passover ceremonial came the later Christian sacrament. Paul may have burdened Christianity with teachings about blood and sacrifice, but by presenting Christ as the last and all-sufficient sacrifice, he made an end once and for all of the doctrine of redemption through sacrifice.
p089.s7.b2: The last section speaks to the modern reader. The consciousness of sin persists, but the old thought patterns of salvation from it have become outworn, and modern man must develop new ways of achieving the consciousness of salvation. The author begins by defining sin anew.

p089.s7.b5: The feeling of guilt is the awareness of having violated the mores; it is not necessarily sin. Indeed, the capacity to recognize guilt is not a mark of human meanness but a badge of a creature of potential greatness, the first stimulus toward the conquests of faith. Confession is a manful repudiation of disloyalty; it does not erase the consequences, but it is essential to spiritual growth.
p089.s8.b0: Paper 89 does not hide humanity’s dark past of taboo, cannibalism, and human sacrifice. But its purpose is not condemnation. It shows how a relationship that began in debt and fear grew, through covenant and symbol, into a relationship of loyalty and trust. Its final section, which sees sin as disloyalty and forgiveness as restored loyalty, invites us to rebuild our relationship with God as one of love rather than bargaining.
